parts.script:
MAYA: Good morning. Riverside Community Garden. How can I help you?

DANIEL: Hi. I'd like to find out about joining. I moved into the area recently, and I'm hoping to do a bit more gardening.

MAYA: Certainly. Let me take a few details first. What's your name?

DANIEL: Daniel Hughes. H-U-G-H-E-S.

MAYA: Thank you, Daniel. And have you found the garden yet?

DANIEL: I think so. Is it the one behind the old library?

MAYA: That's our previous site. We moved two years ago. We're now beside the Riverside Centre, on Mill Road.

DANIEL: Right. I know where that is.

MAYA: Membership is quite straightforward. The annual fee is forty-eight pounds, which covers tools, seeds and basic training.

DANIEL: That's reasonable. How often are members expected to come?

MAYA: Most people join a Saturday afternoon session. We ask each member to attend at least three sessions a month, although you can come more often if you wish.

DANIEL: Do I need to bring my own tools?

MAYA: No. We provide the tools. New members also receive a pair of garden gloves, so you don't need to buy those either.

DANIEL: That's useful. I'm actually hoping to learn rather than just grow things. I've got a small balcony at home and want to get better at growing food.

MAYA: Then you'll fit in well. We have beginners' sessions every month.

DANIEL: Great. What made you set the garden up in the first place?

MAYA: The original aim was to bring neighbours together, but we've gradually added educational activities.

DANIEL: And what happens to everything we grow?

MAYA: Members can take some produce home. Anything left over is sold at the Saturday market, and the money goes back into the garden.

DANIEL: Sounds good. What about access to the tools? Is the shed always open?

MAYA: No. The coordinator opens it at the start of each session and locks it again afterwards. We keep a record of what is taken out.

DANIEL: And if I sign up for Saturday but can't make it one week?

MAYA: Just let us know as soon as possible and ask another member to cover your place. We try not to leave a session short-staffed.

DANIEL: Understood. One last thing. I'm particularly interested in making my own compost. Is that something you teach?

MAYA: Absolutely. Composting is one of our most popular workshops. We run one next month.

DANIEL: Perfect. I think I'll join.

MAYA: Excellent. I'll just give you the registration form...

parts.script:
Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the University Study Hub. I'm Dr Helen Morris, the Student Services Manager, and this short orientation is designed to help you make better use of the building.

The Hub has changed quite a bit this semester. The most important change is that several rooms can now be booked online. You don't have to come to reception simply to reserve a space, although reception staff are still available if you need assistance.

Let me start with the facilities. If you're looking for a quiet place to work alone, the Research Library is the best option. It has individual desks, and the silent-study area is on the upper floor.

If you need to practise a presentation, don't use the library. Instead, book the Media Lab. It has a large screen, recording equipment and adjustable lighting. The Media Lab was moved from its old location because some of the equipment needed better ventilation.

For students who want feedback on an essay, the Writing Centre is the place to go. Advisers won't rewrite your work for you, but they can help you identify problems with structure, argument and academic style.

The Careers Room is where you'll find support for job applications and interviews. If you've never had an interview in English, you can book a practice session there.

The Language Studio is available for language practice, while the Collaboration Lounge is designed for group work. And finally, the Wellbeing Suite provides a quieter space for students who need a break or want to attend a short wellbeing session.

Now, a quick orientation to the building itself. Imagine you're standing at the north entrance. The Research Library is directly ahead of you. If you turn right, you'll find the café. The Writing Centre is beyond the library, on the left-hand side. The Collaboration Lounge is opposite the Writing Centre, near the central staircase. The Careers Room is farther down the same corridor.

The online booking system is particularly useful because the Hub is busiest on Wednesday afternoons. If you're planning group work at that time, book early.

Before you reserve any room, however, I strongly recommend reading the room-use guidelines. Some spaces have restrictions on food, recording or the number of people allowed in them. It will save you time and prevent problems later.

That's all for the main orientation. There are maps available at reception, and the online booking page contains photographs of each room.

parts.script:
NINA: So, are we ready to show Dr Patel the revised plan?

OWEN: I think so. We've narrowed the project down quite a lot.

DR PATEL: Good. I read your first outline. What changed?

NINA: The original question was about whether green roofs improve cities generally. We realised that was far too broad. So now we're asking whether vegetated roofs are associated with lower daytime surface temperatures in the central districts of one city.

DR PATEL: Much better. What exactly will you measure?

OWEN: We thought we'd look at air quality, rainfall and temperature.

DR PATEL: Drop rainfall. It isn't central to your question. Surface temperature is the most direct measure, so make that your primary variable.

NINA: That's what I thought too. I'll handle the temperature sensors.

OWEN: And I'll work with satellite images. They're useful because we can compare a larger number of roofs.

DR PATEL: Exactly. But be careful about assuming the images tell you everything. Some roof surfaces will be difficult to classify.

NINA: We also wanted to use a questionnaire.

DR PATEL: What would you ask?

NINA: Building managers about maintenance, how often the roof is watered, whether plants have been replaced...

DR PATEL: That's useful contextual information. Don't make it your main evidence, though. Treat it as supporting evidence.

OWEN: We've got another problem. Some of the buildings on our list are inaccessible. We can't get permission to put sensors on them.

DR PATEL: Then don't force it. You can use satellite data for those sites, but be transparent about the difference in methods.

NINA: We're especially interested in the difference between vegetated roofs and conventional roofs.

DR PATEL: Good. And remember a crucial distinction in the report: causation and correlation are not the same thing.

OWEN: So even if green roofs are cooler, we can't automatically say the vegetation caused the difference.

DR PATEL: Correct. Other factors, such as building height, roof material or surrounding shade, might contribute.

NINA: When should we start collecting data?

OWEN: We can install the sensors next Monday.

DR PATEL: Fine. Try to take measurements at comparable times of day. Otherwise you'll introduce another source of variation.

OWEN: Should we add another city as a comparison?

DR PATEL: No. Not at this stage. Keep the study focused on one city. A smaller, well-controlled study will be stronger than a rushed comparison.

NINA: That makes sense.

DR PATEL: Good. Revise the methods section, and send it to me before you begin fieldwork.

parts.script:
Good morning. Today I'd like to talk about wayfinding: how people decide where to go and how they construct an understanding of the spaces around them.

For many years, researchers studying navigation focused heavily on maps and landmarks. That work was useful, but it did not fully explain how people navigate in everyday situations. When we move through a familiar environment, we don't necessarily carry a detailed map in our heads.

Instead, people often remember a route as a sequence of actions: leave the station, cross the square, turn left, walk past the bank, and so on. This is efficient because we don't need to analyse the whole environment every time we travel.

However, this strategy has a weakness. Imagine that a road is closed or a familiar shop disappears. Suddenly, the sequence of actions no longer works. The traveller may know perfectly well where the destination is, but the usual route has been interrupted.

This has important implications for the design of public spaces. Signs should reduce the amount of guessing a traveller has to make. A sign that appears too late, uses ambiguous symbols or points in several possible directions creates unnecessary cognitive effort.

This matters particularly for people navigating an unfamiliar environment. Someone who visits a hospital for the first time, for example, cannot depend on the same learned routines as a regular visitor.

Landmarks also play a major role. A landmark is most useful when it is visually distinctive. A large sculpture, unusual building or clearly visible tower may be remembered more easily than a row of identical offices.

There is another distinction worth making. Researchers separate knowing a route from knowing the surrounding environment. A person may be able to travel successfully from A to B without being able to explain where B is in relation to other locations.

Digital navigation has made this distinction even more interesting. Turn-by-turn systems are extremely useful, but because they provide instructions at each stage, they may reduce the need for the traveller to build an internal map. That is not necessarily a problem, but it changes what kind of knowledge the traveller develops.

So, what does good wayfinding design look like? There is no single answer. A well-designed environment combines clear signs, distinctive landmarks, consistent visual information and, increasingly, digital assistance.

For inclusive design, information should also be available through more than one channel. Visual signs are important, but audible announcements, tactile information and accessible digital tools can support people who cannot use one particular form of information effectively.

The central point, then, is that navigation is not simply a matter of reading a map. Human wayfinding involves memory, action, perception and decision-making. The most effective systems recognise that people use these sources of information together.

parts.title: Introduction and Interview
parts.examinerInstructions: Begin with identity confirmation and a brief introduction. Ask questions in a natural conversational manner. Use the selected topic set; do not ask every question if timing is reached.

questions: Are you working or are you a student?
What do you enjoy most about your studies?
Is there anything you find difficult about studying?
How do you usually prepare for an important examination?
Do you think your approach to learning has changed as you have become older?
How often do you use technology during the day?
What piece of technology do you use most?
Has technology changed the way you communicate with people?
Is there any technology you would find difficult to live without?
Do you think people rely too much on technology?
What is your neighbourhood like?
What place do you enjoy visiting there?
Are there any places you would like to see improved?
Do you prefer spending time in busy places or quiet places?
How might your area change in the future?

assessment.overallCalculation: Average the four criterion scores; round to the nearest whole or half band according to IELTS-style rounding.

bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.9: Expert: fluent, precise, highly flexible; wide and natural vocabulary; highly accurate grammar; effortless intelligibility.
bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.8: Very strong: fluent with only occasional hesitation; wide vocabulary and flexible structures; generally accurate; easy to understand.
bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.7: Good: can speak at length with some hesitation; sufficient range for precise meaning; generally controlled grammar; pronunciation supports communication.
bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.6: Competent: can sustain a conversation but may show repetition, hesitation or limited flexibility; adequate vocabulary; mix of simple and complex structures with errors that rarely impede communication.
bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.5: Modest: can maintain basic communication but relies on repetition and limited structures; vocabulary may be insufficient for precision; errors may cause some difficulty.
bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.4: Limited: frequent pauses and reformulation; limited vocabulary and grammar; pronunciation may cause frequent difficulty.
bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.3: Extremely limited: communicates only basic ideas with frequent breakdowns.
bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.2: Intermittent: very little communicative language beyond isolated words or memorised expressions.
bandDescriptorOperationalGuidance.1: Non-user: essentially no ability to use language beyond isolated words.
